extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, and students/scholars of journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for how journalists and editors select, evaluate, and manage sources for news stories (including logistical, social, and organizational constraints). Focuses on national newsroom and magazine production practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational clarity and concision in magazine writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Assembling information from several files around a framework that flows logically, with the fewest number of words and without repetition or resort to unnecessary bridges that may add to story length or sound hackneyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers must organize material so that it flows; avoid repetition and clichéd transitions; meet agreed-on story length; galley fitting may require adding or cutting lines. Cover stories may be rewritten several times; senior and top editors routinely edit for content and length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial revision, page-allocation, and section makeup
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior editors and top editors review and revise stories, decide section order and which stories receive color photographs, and manage total page requirements — appealing for or reallocating pages when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senior editors plan section makeup by Day 4/5, may appeal to top editors for more pages (front-of-book appeals usually granted), and must cut or kill sections if pages are insufficient. Final decisions rest with top editors; front-of-book flow and breaking events can change makeup up to press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinants of a source's ability to gain access
rubrics_metrics.description: A source's successful access to journalists is shaped by four interrelated factors: (1) incentives, (2) power, (3) the ability to supply suitable information, and (4) geographic and social proximity to journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All four factors interact; ability to supply suitable information is crucial but is enhanced by incentives, power, and proximity. Editors and reporters assess sources along these dimensions when selecting whom to use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source incentives: eager, agreeable, and recalcitrant
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources differ by incentive: eager sources actively seek publicity (depend on media), agreeable sources cooperate but don't need publicity, and recalcitrant sources refuse access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News is weighted toward eager sources who benefit from publicity. Recalcitrant sources (e.g., organized crime, covert agencies) appear mainly when arrested or exposed; refusing access can prompt investigative reporting, which is costly and used selectively. Reporters sometimes pursue recalcitrant sources extensively when story payoff justifies effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of sources and burden of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful sources can bar access and exercise primary censorship; stories about powerful actors often require considerable evidence before executives will defend publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powerful institutions (e.g., White House, Pentagon) may withhold access citing national security. When reporting on powerful sources, reporters must secure strong substantiation to withstand pushback and protect themselves from dismissal; declining access can itself increase journalistic hunger for a story (possible exposes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to supply suitable information (quality, exclusives, and saturation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources that can supply suitable, well-packaged information (exclusives, accessible spokespeople, timely materials) gain advantage; some organizations can 'saturate' media with information to crowd out less-resourced sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies that provide detailed leaks or exclusives (FBI, DEA examples) can shape news to serve their interests. Large organizations can preschedule activities, provide film clips, spokespeople on short notice, and send handouts—advantages especially when newsrooms lack resources. Journalists should be alert to organizational motives; nonpayment for sources produces class-related selection bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment and identification of media events and pseudo-events
rubrics_metrics.description: Events staged primarily for media coverage ('media events' or 'pseudo-events') can be newsworthy, but journalists are wary of being 'used' and should identify staged activities when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all staged events are newsworthy; journalists may refuse coverage if they suspect manipulation (e.g., staged demonstrations). However, a blanket taboo on pseudo-events would leave news holes; small or marginalized groups may need staged events to reach audiences. Journalists should expose when events are created for media effect. Staging by journalists is prohibited; restaging to improve story quality is permissible but hoaxes/staging that damages credibility are punished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic proximity and bureau/stringer coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic proximity — presence of bureaus and wire-service stringers — influences which stories and sources are available to national news organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domestic news clusters around bureau locations; many rural or low-income areas remain uncovered. Establish bureaus when a critical mass of stories arises. Geographic gaps create systematic coverage blind spots that shape national news agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social proximity and source representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Social closeness between journalists and potential sources (class, race, age, social networks) strongly affects which sources are contactable and therefore who appears in the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists tend to select sources similar to themselves or those reachable via peer/personal networks, producing bias toward upper-middle-class and familiar constituencies. Special efforts (e.g., using community organizations, hiring local reporters) are needed to reach working-class or marginalized populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of peer and personal sources as heuristics for availability and audience interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior publication in peer outlets and personal contacts are used as quick signals that a topic is available and likely to interest audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors scan other media for 'angles' and use established outlets (e.g., New York Times) as guarantors of professional judgment. Personal sources (family, friends) supply credible, audience-representative tips. Relying on peers and personal networks is efficient but can reinforce homogeneity of topics and perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistical feasibility and timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical logistics — personnel, cameras, film transmission, and scheduling — determine whether a desired story can be covered and used by news organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical failures (broken cameras, bad film, transportation delays) and limited crews can cause newsrooms to lose stories. Networks are more vulnerable to such constraints than magazines. These logistical limits are rarely publicized but shape post-mortem production decisions and staffing reorganizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency in source selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists apply source considerations aiming for efficiency: obtain the most suitable news from the fewest number of sources as quickly, easily, and cheaply as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With tight deadlines and limited budgets, reporters prioritize sources that yield high informational payoff with minimal resource expenditure. This pragmatic efficiency influences decisions about whom to contact, how to verify, and when to pursue investigative work.
